# Abstract

The Guiana Shield between the Orinoco and Amazon deltas constituted one of the
most distinct demographic and environmental frontiers of early modern European
expansion. Spanning 453.932 km² across four colonial jurisdictions (Essequibo and
Demerara, Berbice and the Interior, Dutch Suriname, and French Guiana), the
region experienced an initial demographic contraction from an indigenous
aggregate of approximately 193.000 inhabitants in 1595AD down to a secular nadir
of 122.000 in 1700AD. Introduced Old World pathogens, enslavement and violent
dislocation along interior river basins eroded native Lokono (Arawak), Kali'na
(Carib), Akawaio and Wayampi populations before European settlements achieved
demographic stability.

From the early eighteenth century, demographic trajectories reversed through the
massive introduction of enslaved African labourers and the transfer of Dutch
hydraulic empoldering technology from Zeeland to the maritime coastal clays.
Between 1700AD and 1815AD, total population expanded from 122.000 to 224.000,
concentrating heavily along narrow coastal strips and tidal river mouths. While
French Guiana remained constrained by ecological headwinds, fiscal neglect and
the catastrophic failure of the 1763AD Kourou settlement scheme, Dutch Suriname
and the western colonies of Essequibo, Demerara and Berbice emerged as intensive
plantation economies producing sugar, coffee and cotton.

Simultaneously, the vast rainforest interior supported autonomous African Maroon
polities (Ndyuka, Saramaka, Matawai and Aluku) who established independent
sovereignty through armed resistance and formal peace treaties with the Dutch
colonial state in 1760AD and 1762AD. Across the western Guianas, the transfer of
Essequibo, Demerara and Berbice to British dominion during the Napoleonic Wars,
formalised by the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1814 and the Congress of Vienna in
1815AD, inaugurated an intense phase of British capital investment and polder
consolidation that established Demerara as the premier sugar-producing colony of
the nineteenth-century Caribbean littoral.

# Spatial Framework and the Four Guiana Shield Polities

The geographical domain of the colonial Guianas comprises the coastal lowlands
and crystalline uplands of the north-eastern Guiana Shield, bounded to the west
by the Orinoco drainage divide, to the south by the Tumuc-Humac and Acarai
mountain ranges, and to the east by the Oyapock River bordering Portuguese
Amazonia [@goslinga1985dutch; @scammacca2022geodiversity]. The total land surface
encompasses 453.932 km², partitioned into four historical jurisdictions that
reflect competitive European mercantilist expansion and distinct ecological
adaptations.

The first macro-region, Essequibo and Demerara (131.771 km²), encompasses the
broad alluvial estuaries of the Essequibo, Cuyuni, Mazaruni and Demerara rivers.
Initially settled by Zeeland traders operating under the Dutch West India
Company (WIC) in the early seventeenth century, the colony was anchored at Fort
Kyk-Over-Al at the confluence of the Essequibo, Mazaruni and Cuyuni rivers
[@hartsinck1770beschryving; @thompson1987colonialism]. During the directorship of
Laurens Storm van 's Gravesande (1743AD to 1772AD), European settlement relocated
decisively from upriver trading posts down to the fertile coastal mudflats and
the Demerara River estuary, where British planters quickly came to dominate land
clearing and sugar cane cultivation [@goslinga1985dutch; @higman1984slave].

The second macro-region, Berbice and Interior Guyana (93.196 km²), covers the
Berbice and Canje river basins together with the expansive interior plateaus of
the Pakaraima Mountains and the Rupununi savannahs. Founded in 1627AD by Abraham
van Pere as a proprietary feudal colony, Berbice passed to the Society of
Berbice (*Sociëteit van Berbice*) in 1720AD [@hartsinck1770beschryving].
Settlement remained clustered along the middle reaches of the Berbice River
surrounding Fort Nassau until the massive slave rebellion of 1763AD destroyed the
upriver plantation zone, prompting a late-eighteenth-century relocation towards
the coast and the founding of New Amsterdam in 1791AD
[@thompson1987colonialism].

The third macro-region, Dutch Suriname and Maroon Polities (144.791 km²), covers
the Suriname, Commewijne, Cottica, Saramacca and Coppename river systems.
Acquired by the Dutch Republic from England under the Treaty of Breda in 1667AD,
the colony was administered from 1683AD by the Society of Suriname (*Sociëteit
van Suriname*), a tripartite corporate syndicate comprising the WIC, the City of
Amsterdam and the noble family of Van Aerssen van Sommelsdijck
[@goslinga1985dutch; @oostindie2005paradise]. The colony developed the most
capital-intensive plantation complex on the South American mainland, while its
forested interior became home to sovereign Maroon federations including the
Saramaka and Ndyuka [@price1983firsttime; @vanstipriaan1993surinaams].

The fourth macro-region, French Guiana (84.174 km²), extends from the Maroni
River eastward to the Oyapock River, centred on the island of Cayenne and the
coastal plains of Kourou and Sinnamary [@mamlamfouck1992histoire;
@cardoso1999guyane]. First permanently occupied by French expeditions under the
Compagnie de la France Équinoxiale in 1643AD, French Guiana struggled with
chronic metropolitan underfunding, severe tropical disease mortality, and
recurrent Dutch and Portuguese naval incursions [@palisse2022living;
@auger2018creating].

# Demographic Trajectory: Contact Contraction, Sugar Empoldering and Late Boom

The historical demography of the colonial Guianas from 1595AD to 1815AD displays
an asymmetric U-shaped trajectory, declining from an initial indigenous baseline
of 193.000 down to a trough of 122.000 in 1700AD, before rebounding through
transatlantic slave imports to reach 224.000 at the conclusion of the Napoleonic
Wars. Table \ref{tab:trajectories} documents this macro-regional population
reconstruction across seven benchmark dates.

The initial decline of 36,8% between 1595AD and 1700AD reflected severe
epidemiological mortality among coastal Amerindian populations following regular
contact with European privateers, Dutch traders and Spanish expeditions
operating from the Orinoco basin [@whitehead1988lords; @whitehead1997discoverie].
Smallpox, influenza and respiratory infections devastated village networks along
the Essequibo, Corentyne and Maroni rivers. By 1700AD, the native populations of
the immediate coastal zone had contracted dramatically, forcing European
settlers to import enslaved African labourers to sustain nascent sugar and
tobacco plantations [@goslinga1985dutch; @postma1990dutch].

The eighteenth century witnessed a complete restructuring of the demographic
base. Driven by Dutch merchant capital and transatlantic slaving voyages
organised by the Middelburgsche Commercie Compagnie (MCC) and the WIC, enslaved
Africans became the overwhelming majority of the population in Suriname,
Essequibo, Demerara and Berbice [@postma1990dutch; @vanstipriaan1993surinaams].
Between 1700AD and 1780AD, the population of Dutch Suriname rose from 42.000 to
76.000, while Essequibo and Demerara expanded from 35.000 to 58.000.

Table \ref{tab:subreg-summary} summarises the geographic and demographic status
of the four polities at the benchmark of 1815AD, illustrating the stark disparity
between the densely settled Anglo-Dutch plantation zones and the sparsely
populated French territory.

Figure \ref{fig:trajectory} highlights the divergence in regional growth
trajectories. Essequibo and Demerara experienced an explosive expansion from
1780AD onward, surpassing Dutch Suriname around 1800AD to reach 92.000
inhabitants in 1815AD, propelled by British capital injections, high slave
importation rates, and superior coastal polder productivity [@higman1984slave;
@thompson1987colonialism].

# Essequibo and Demerara: From River Trading Posts to Atlantic Polder Boom

The historical demography of Essequibo and Demerara divides into two distinct
phases: an early upriver mercantile phase lasting from 1616AD to approximately
1745AD, followed by an intensive downstream coastal polder boom from 1745AD to
1815AD [@hartsinck1770beschryving; @goslinga1985dutch].

During the initial phase, Dutch merchants focused on barter trade with
indigenous communities rather than agricultural production. The headquarters of
the WIC Commandeur was located at Fort Kyk-Over-Al, a tiny island fortress at the
juncture of the Essequibo, Mazaruni and Cuyuni rivers [@thompson1987colonialism].
Early plantations were established on the upriver riverbanks, where soils were
sandy and easily tilled but suffered rapid nutrient leaching. The total colonial
population in 1700AD stood at only 35.000, consisting largely of dispersed
interior Amerindian groups and fewer than 3.000 enslaved Africans and European
traders [@whitehead1988lords; @goslinga1985dutch].

The transformative turn occurred under Laurens Storm van 's Gravesande, who
served as Commandeur and subsequently Director-General of Essequibo and Demerara
from 1743AD to 1772AD. Recognising the exhaustion of the upriver estates,
Gravesande opened the lower reaches of the Demerara River to settlement in
1746AD and invited foreign planters, primarily British subjects from Barbados,
Antigua and Saint Kitts, to acquire land concessions [@hartsinck1770beschryving;
@goslinga1985dutch]. The British brought substantial liquid capital and large
slaving retinues, rapidly outstripping Dutch settlers in both numbers and output.
By 1760AD, Demerara had surpassed Essequibo in economic importance and enslaved
population [@thompson1987colonialism].

The coastal transformation required Dutch hydraulic engineering. The rich
alluvial mudflats along the Atlantic coast, composed of heavy pegasse and marine
clays, lay beneath high-tide level and were subject to severe flooding. Drawing
on Zeeland reclamation techniques, planters constructed earthen sea dams along
the coast, excavated massive drainage canals, and installed timber sluice gates
(*kokers*) that allowed freshwater run-off to discharge into the sea at low tide
while barring the entrance of ocean salt water at high tide
[@vanstipriaan1993surinaams; @palisse2022living]. These polders yielded
unprecedented sugar cane harvests, with sucrose yields per acre doubling those
of the older British Caribbean islands [@higman1984slave].

The administrative centre shifted downriver to reflect this coastal economic
gravity. In 1782AD, during the French occupation of the colony in the American
Revolutionary War, French engineers laid out a new capital near the mouth of the
Demerara River, initially named La Nouvelle Ville, which the Dutch renamed
Stabroek in 1784AD in honour of Nicolaas Geelvinck, Lord of Castricum and
President of the WIC [@hartsinck1770beschryving]. Following British seizure in
1796AD and permanent acquisition in 1814AD, the town was rechristened Georgetown
in 1812AD in honour of King George III. By 1815AD, Georgetown had expanded into a
bustling mercantile port of 45.100 inhabitants, serving as the commercial node
for 216 catalogued plantations, cotton estates and parish districts across the
two river valleys [@higman1984slave].

# Berbice and the Interior Frontier: The 1763 Slave Uprising and Downriver Migration

The colony of Berbice developed on a distinct institutional footing as a private
proprietary charter granted to Abraham van Pere in 1627AD. In 1720AD, the Van
Pere family transferred their rights to the newly incorporated Society of
Berbice, which opened the colony to general investment and imported increased
numbers of enslaved labourers [@hartsinck1770beschryving]. Settlement in Berbice
remained concentrated far upriver, between 50 and 80 kilometres from the
Atlantic coast, along the Berbice and Canje rivers surrounding the administrative
hub of Fort Nassau [@thompson1987colonialism].

Berbice plantations operated under exceptional fiscal austerity and harsh labour
discipline. When epidemics of dysentery and malaria broke out in the late 1750s,
striking both European overseers and enslaved workers, planters reduced food
rations and intensified punishment. On 23 February 1763AD, an enslaved man named
Coffy (Cuffy) from plantation Magdalenenburg on the Canje River initiated an
insurrection that expanded into the largest slave rebellion in the history of the
Guianas [@thompson1987colonialism; @goslinga1985dutch].

The rebels quickly captured estates along the Canje and Berbice rivers, driving
surviving European colonists into Fort Nassau. Governor Wolfert Simon van
Hoogenheim, lacking adequate munitions and military personnel, evacuated the
fort and set it on fire on 8 March 1763AD, retreating downstream to Fort Sint
Andries at the river mouth. For over twelve months, Coffy established an
autonomous revolutionary administration across Berbice, styling himself Governor
and organising agricultural production to feed his army [@thompson1987colonialism].
However, internal factional conflict between Coffy and his lieutenant Atta,
combined with an acute shortage of provisions and the arrival of twelve Dutch
naval vessels carrying European soldiers from Suriname and the Netherlands,
eroded the uprising. Assisted by Carib and Arawak warriors who attacked the rebel
encampments from the forest flanks, Dutch forces re-established control by the
middle of 1764AD [@whitehead1988lords; @goslinga1985dutch].

The rebellion devastated the demographic and material infrastructure of Berbice.
Over half of the enslaved population perished from combat, starvation, disease
and judicial executions, while numerous estates were reduced to ashes. The
colony's population contracted sharply, recovering only slowly from 25.000 in
1750AD to 28.000 in 1780AD. Recognising the defensive vulnerability and soil
exhaustion of the upriver plantations, the Society of Berbice abandoned Fort
Nassau and founded a new coastal capital, New Amsterdam, in 1791AD at the
confluence of the Berbice and Canje rivers [@thompson1987colonialism].

In the vast interior beyond the plantation zone, Berbice bordered the Pakaraima
Mountains and the Rupununi savannahs. These interior plateaus remained under the
effective control of autonomous Amerindian nations, including the Macushi,
Wapishana and Patamona [@whitehead1988lords]. The Dutch colonial authorities
maintained formal diplomatic relations through Dutch postholders (*bijzitters*)
stationed at remote interior river posts such as Arinda on the upper Essequibo.
These postholders distributed trade goods (iron knives, axes, textiles and beads)
in exchange for cassava flour, hunting dogs, letterwood and military assistance
in capturing runaway slaves, creating a stable buffer zone against Spanish
encroachment from the Orinoco missions [@whitehead1988lords; @price2014vizinhos].

# Dutch Suriname: Society of Suriname, Polder Agro-Capitalism and Maroon Treaties

Dutch Suriname represented the economic and institutional centrepiece of the
eighteenth-century Dutch Caribbean empire [@oostindie2005paradise;
@goslinga1985dutch]. After acquiring the territory from England in 1667AD, the
States of Zeeland initially struggled to govern the territory, leading to the
creation in 1683AD of the Society of Suriname (*Sociëteit van Suriname*). Under
the leadership of Cornelis van Aerssen van Sommelsdijck, who governed from
1683AD until his assassination by mutinous soldiers in 1688AD, the colony
established a rigid institutional architecture combining civil administration,
coastal drainage works and massive slave imports [@goslinga1985dutch].

Suriname developed an extraordinarily intensive plantation belt along the lower
Suriname, Commewijne, Cottica and Saramacca rivers. Planters empoldered tidal
swamps with complex dykes, canals and sluices, creating expansive estates
averaging 150 to 300 enslaved workers [@vanstipriaan1993surinaams]. Sugar cane
dominated early production, supplemented from the 1720s by coffee, cacao and
cotton. A prominent element of the planter class was the Portuguese and German
Sephardic Jewish community, who established an autonomous agricultural settlement
at Jodensavanne on the upper Suriname River, complete with their own communal
court, militia and the synagogue Beracha ve Shalom, erected in 1685AD
[@goslinga1985dutch].

The extreme brutality of plantation labour regimes in Suriname produced
unsustainable demographic deficits. Mortality rates among enslaved workers
consistently exceeded birth rates by 2% to 4% annually, necessitating a
continuous inflow of newly captured Africans from the Atlantic slave trade to
maintain the labour force [@lamur1987demographic; @vanstipriaan1993surinaams;
@postma1990dutch]. Between 1668AD and 1815AD, Dutch merchants transported over
215.000 enslaved Africans to Suriname. Yet the colony's total population grew
from only 42.000 in 1700AD to 76.000 in 1780AD, reflecting the massive human
depletion caused by overwork, malnutrition, tropical fevers and punishment
[@lamur1987demographic; @oostindie2005paradise].

The harsh regime provoked endemic desertion into the tropical rainforest.
Runaway slaves (*Marroons* or *Maroons*, known historically as *Bosnegers*)
established nucleated communities in the interior, mastering the rapids, swamp
navigation and subsistence agriculture [@price1983firsttime; @price1976maroon].
Maroon women played a critical role in agricultural adaptation, cultivating
African rice varieties (*Oryza glaberrima*) and traditional root crops that
sustained interior forest settlements [@vanandel2023maroon; @pinas2023vernacular].

Faced with escalating plantation raids that threatened the financial viability of
the colony, the Dutch colonial administration conducted repeated military
expeditions into the interior, but European troops suffered debilitating losses
from ambush and tropical illness. Recognising the military stalemate, the
Society of Suriname concluded formal peace treaties with the principal Maroon
nations: the Ndyuka (Djuka) on the Tapanahoni and Marowijne rivers in 1760AD, the
Saramaka on the upper Suriname River in 1762AD, and the Matawai on the Saramacca
River in 1767AD [@price1983firsttime; @price1976maroon].

These treaties recognised the territorial autonomy and sovereign freedom of the
Maroon federations, provided annual tribute in metal tools, firearms and
textiles, and established defined boundary limits beyond which European troops
could not advance. In return, the Maroons agreed to cease raiding plantations and
to apprehend and return future runaway slaves. However, a dissident group, the
Aluku (Boni) Maroons led by Boni and Baron, refused submission, fighting a
protracted guerrilla conflict known as the Boni Wars (1768AD to 1793AD) against
Dutch colonial forces and European mercenary corps before retreating across the
Maroni River into French territory [@price1976maroon; @anderson1980recent;
@gugolati2023collectivity].

Suriname's plantation economy reached its financial zenith in the 1760s before
suffering a catastrophic credit crash in 1773AD. Known as the Amsterdam mortgage
crisis (*Surinaamse hypotheekcrisis*), excessive borrowing by absentee planters
led to mass foreclosures, financial panic, and the transfer of estate
ownership to Dutch merchant banking houses [@vanstipriaan1993surinaams;
@oostindie2005paradise]. The colony stagnated demographically, slipping from
76.000 in 1780AD to 72.000 in 1815AD, as British Demerara captured the Atlantic
sugar trade.

# French Guiana: Cayenne and the 1763 Kourou Expedition

French Guiana stood apart from its Dutch neighbours in its demographic fragility,
modest agricultural output and recurrent administrative reorganisations
[@mamlamfouck1992histoire; @cardoso1999guyane]. First colonised by the
Compagnie de Rouen in 1643AD, the settlement on the Île de Cayenne suffered
constant harassment from Dutch privateers, Carib warriors and Portuguese forces
from the Amazon [@palisse2022living]. By 1700AD, the colony contained only
23.000 inhabitants, consisting predominantly of unassimilated native groups in
the interior and approximately 2.500 French settlers and enslaved Africans
concentrated around Fort Cépérou in Cayenne [@cardoso1999guyane].

The most productive agricultural enterprises in early French Guiana were
developed by religious orders, particularly the Society of Jesus. Operating from
1668AD until their royal expulsion in 1763AD, the Jesuits established extensive
sugar, cacao and coffee plantations along the coastal savannahs and tidal
estuaries of Remire-Montjoly, Macouria and Sinnamary [@auger2018creating]. Their
flagship estate, the Habitation Loyola at Remire, utilised innovative watermills
and industrial pottery works, employing several hundred enslaved labourers who
were housed in structured quarters and subjected to strict religious
supervision [@auger2018creating; @tareau2019wild].

Following the loss of New France (Canada) in the Seven Years' War by the Treaty
of Paris in 1763AD, the French Secretary of State for the Navy, Étienne-François,
Duc de Choiseul, sought to construct a new tropical empire in South America.
Choiseul devised a grandiose scheme to populate the coastal savannahs between
Kourou and Sinnamary with free European peasant farmers, bypassing the reliance
on enslaved African labour that characterised British and Dutch colonies
[@mamlamfouck1992histoire; @cardoso1999guyane].

Between 1763AD and 1765AD, metropolitan recruiters enlisted over 12.000
immigrants from Alsace, Lorraine, the Rhineland, Switzerland and Acadia,
promising free land, provisions and tools in the Expedition of Kourou. The
undertaking proved one of the most disastrous colonial ventures in Atlantic
history. When the ships arrived off the coast of French Guiana, the colonial
administration under the Chevalier de Turgot and Jean-Baptiste Thibault de
Chanvalon had made virtually no preparations for their reception [@cardoso1999guyane;
@fuggle2021toxic].

Thousands of European migrants were dumped on the open beaches of Kourou without
potable water, adequate shelter or sanitary infrastructure. The arrival coincided
with torrential equatorial rains that transformed the coastal plain into a
morass. Epidemics of typhus, yellow fever, malaria and bacterial dysentery ripped
through the encampments. Within eighteen months, between 7.000 and 9.000 settlers
perished from disease and starvation, while several thousand survivors were
evacuated back to France [@cardoso1999guyane; @fuggle2021toxic; @dupont2026kokobe].
A small remnant found refuge on the offshore volcanic islands of the Îles du
Diable, which, because they offered fresh ocean breezes and fewer disease
vectors, were renamed the Îles du Salut (*Salvation Islands*) [@fuggle2021toxic;
@forsdick2020between].

The Kourou disaster shattered French metropolitan confidence in Guiana, leaving
the colony branded as a pestilential graveyard. Subsequent governors, notably
the Swiss-born engineer Pierre-Victor Malouet and the Chevalier de Fiedmond,
attempted to restore the colony by reverting to traditional enslaved plantation
agriculture and introducing spice cultivation (clove, nutmeg and cinnamon)
smuggled from the Dutch East Indies [@cardoso1999guyane; @tareau2020phytotherapies].
However, the plantation economy remained anaemic. During the French Revolution,
the National Convention abolished slavery in 1794AD and transformed Cayenne into
a deportation centre for refractory Catholic priests and royalist dissidents,
earning the colony the grim sobriquet of the Dry Guillotine (*la guillotine
sèche*) [@forsdick2020between; @fuggle2025enduring].

Napoleon re-established slavery in 1802AD, provoking abortive local resistance,
before Anglo-Portuguese forces operating from Belém do Pará invaded and captured
Cayenne in 1809AD [@cardoso1999guyane; @reno2016dichotomy]. French Guiana
remained under Portuguese occupation until returned to France following the
Treaty of Paris in 1814AD and the Congress of Vienna in 1815AD. At the benchmark
of 1815AD, French Guiana remained the smallest and most fragile of the four
polities, numbering only 24.000 inhabitants across 36 catalogued settlements,
with Cayenne housing 6.100 residents [@cardoso1999guyane; @palisse2022living].

# Amerindian Demographic Trajectories and Forest Borderlands

The demographic trajectory of indigenous Amerindians in the colonial Guianas
was characterized by initial collapse followed by ethnogenetic restructuring and
strategic adaptation to European trading networks [@whitehead1988lords;
@renaultlescure2009loanwords]. Prior to European contact in 1595AD, the coastal
strip and lower river basins supported substantial populations of Arawak
(Lokono) and Carib (Kali'na or Galibi) horticulturalists, while the interior
shield uplands were inhabited by Akawaio, Patamona, Macushi, Wapishana, Wai-Wai,
Wayana and Wayampi groups [@whitehead1988lords; @price2014vizinhos].

Sir Walter Ralegh's expedition of 1595AD in search of Manoa (El Dorado)
documented complex inter-tribal confederations across the Essequibo, Cuyuni and
Orinoco basins capable of fielding hundreds of war canoes [@whitehead1997discoverie].
However, the establishment of permanent European trading factories in the early
seventeenth century introduced recurring epidemic cycles. By 1700AD, the coastal
Amerindian population had fallen by over 40%, retreating from the tidal mangroves
into the interior savannahs and river headwaters [@whitehead1988lords].

Despite this aggregate contraction, Amerindian nations maintained critical
geopolitical leverage throughout the eighteenth century. Both Dutch and French
authorities found it impossible to expand beyond their coastal polders without
indigenous military cooperation. In Essequibo, Demerara and Berbice, the Dutch
formalised alliances with the Caribs and Arawaks, recognising their status as
free persons immune from colonial enslavement [@whitehead1988lords;
@thompson1987colonialism]. In exchange for firearms, gunpowder, iron axes and
cloth, Carib war parties served as colonial border auxiliaries, suppressing
plantation slave insurrections (as in Berbice in 1763AD) and tracking fugitive
slaves in the deep forest [@whitehead1988lords; @price2014vizinhos].

In French Guiana, Kali'na communities along the Maroni, Mana and Sinnamary
rivers developed extensive linguistic and economic exchanges with French
settlers and Catholic missionaries, incorporating French and Dutch loanwords
into their vocabulary while preserving traditional matrilineal kinship structures
and slash-and-burn manioc cultivation [@renaultlescure2009loanwords;
@tareau2019wild]. In the far interior, the Wayana and Wayampi controlled the
trans-shield portage routes connecting the Maroni and Oyapock basins to the Jari
and Amazon drainages, retaining de facto independence from both French and
Portuguese colonial authority well past the close of the eighteenth century
[@scammacca2022geodiversity; @palisse2022living].

# Settlement Toponymy, Spatial Gazetteers and Archival Reconciliation

The settlement gazetteer compiled for the colonial Guianas reconciles 466
catalogued localities across the four polities against authentic archival rolls,
historical cartography and administrative tax records [@hartsinck1770beschryving;
@higman1984slave; @thompson1987colonialism; @vanstipriaan1993surinaams;
@cardoso1999guyane]. The toponymic landscape reflects the layered cultural and
institutional history of the region.

In Essequibo, Demerara and Berbice, settlement names preserve the Dutch
mercantile legacy (Vreed-en-Hoop, Schoonord, Zeeburg, Anna Regina, Uitvlugt,
Nieuw Amsterdam, Fort Nassau), overlaid by British plantation nomenclature
(Windsor Forest, Bel Air, Enterprise, Albion, Providence, Port Mourant) and
indigenous river designations (Bartica, Mahaica, Mahaicony, Corentyne,
Rupununi, Canje) [@thompson1987colonialism; @higman1984slave].

In Dutch Suriname, toponyms capture the corporate empoldering projects along the
Commewijne, Cottica and Saramacca rivers (Mariënburg, Domburg, Alkmaar,
Groningen, Meerzorg, Bakkie, Nieuw-Amsterdam), alongside the enduring Sephardic
heritage of Jodensavanne and traditional Maroon riverside settlements along the
Tapanahoni and Upper Suriname rivers (Asidonhopo, Drietabbetje, Langatabbetje,
Paloemeu) [@price1983firsttime; @vanstipriaan1993surinaams].

In French Guiana, the toponymy combines Catholic patron saints and missionary
reserves (Saint-Georges, Saint-Laurent-du-Maroni, Saint-Élie, Remire-Montjoly)
with native toponyms adapted into French phonology (Cayenne, Kourou, Sinnamary,
Iracoubo, Camopi, Oyapock, Approuague) and revolutionary geographic markers
[@mamlamfouck1992histoire; @cardoso1999guyane; @palisse2022living].

All 466 catalogued settlements in the gazetteer database reconcile cleanly
against the source ledger without duplication or geographic distortion. By
integrating geographic coordinates, administrative jurisdictions, foundation
dates and longitudinal population estimates from 1595AD to 1815AD, this spatial
reconstruction establishes a rigorous empirical foundation for historical
demography across the Guiana Shield.
